The essential answer

What is BMI?

Body Mass Index (BMI) is a weight-for-height screening measure. For adults, it is calculated from weight and height and grouped into broad categories that can help flag possible health risk. It does not measure body fat directly.

BMI is one of the most familiar numbers in preventive health. It is used in clinics, public-health research, and everyday healthy weight calculators because it is inexpensive, reproducible, and easy to understand. The number is useful precisely because it is simple: it relates body weight to height. But that simplicity is also its limit. A BMI result is a starting point for a conversation about health, not a verdict on a person’s health, appearance, or worth.

BMI formula: metric and imperial

The metric BMI formula is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. If someone weighs 70 kg and is 1.70 m tall, their calculation is 70 ÷ (1.70 × 1.70), or 24.2. The imperial formula uses pounds and inches: weight in pounds × 703 ÷ height in inches squared. Both produce the same BMI Index when the measurements are converted correctly.

Adult BMICategoryGeneral interpretation
Below 18.5UnderweightMay need individual assessment
18.5–24.9Healthy weightGenerally lowest population-level risk
25.0–29.9OverweightPotentially increased risk
30.0 and aboveObesityIncreased risk; support may help

Why clinicians use BMI categories

At the population level, BMI categories are associated with different rates of conditions such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnoea, and cardiovascular disease. This makes BMI a helpful first screen. In an individual appointment, a clinician may pair it with blood pressure, blood tests, waist circumference, family history, medications, diet, physical activity, and the direction of weight change over time.

A single BMI cannot tell you whether you have a medical condition. Nor can it tell you where weight is carried. Abdominal fat is particularly relevant to cardiometabolic risk, which is why a waist measurement can be helpful. If your BMI result is unexpected, sudden, or worrying, it deserves context rather than self-judgment.

BMI scale and healthy body weight

The usual adult BMI scale identifies 18.5 to 24.9 as the healthy weight range. Our calculator translates that range into a practical weight interval for your height. That interval is not an “ideal” body shape and it is not a target to pursue at all costs. Healthy body weight looks different across life stages, cultures, body frames, and medical histories. For many adults, improving blood pressure, stamina, sleep, or food habits matters more than reaching a particular number on the scale.

BMI for women and BMI for men

Standard adult BMI categories are the same for women and men. Nonetheless, people with the same BMI can have different proportions of fat and lean tissue. Hormonal changes, pregnancy, menopause, and life stage can shape weight distribution for women. Men may carry more weight around the abdomen. These differences are reasons to broaden the health picture, not reasons to treat the calculation as irrelevant. Visit our BMI for women guide or BMI for men guide for a fuller discussion.

BMI by age: adults, seniors, and children

For adults, the categories do not change with age. In later life, however, unintentional weight loss, reduced muscle mass, falls, chronic illness, and frailty make the story more nuanced. Older adults benefit from individualized advice that protects strength, protein intake, mobility, and independence. BMI for children is different again. Children and teenagers are assessed using BMI-for-age growth charts and percentiles, not adult cutoffs. A paediatric clinician can interpret those charts in the context of growth and development.

When BMI is less informative

Athletes and people with substantial muscle mass can have a higher BMI without having excess body fat. Pregnancy, fluid retention, limb loss, and some medical conditions can also affect the meaning of the number. Ethnicity can matter as well: some populations experience metabolic risks at lower BMI levels. The best next step may be a clinician’s assessment, waist measurement, body-composition test, or simply a discussion of symptoms and lifestyle.

BMI versus body fat percentage

BMI uses only height and weight. Body fat percentage estimates how much of body weight is fat tissue. That extra detail can be useful, but measurement methods vary in accuracy. Home scales using bioelectrical impedance can change with hydration. Skinfold measurements and DEXA scans require technique or equipment. For most people, a consistent trend in multiple measures is more useful than a single supposedly perfect number.

A healthy weight plan built around habits

If you would like to gain, lose, or maintain weight, begin with habits you can repeat. Eat regular meals with vegetables or fruit, fibre-rich carbohydrates, protein, and fats that fit your culture and budget. Make water your default drink. Plan movement you enjoy: brisk walking, cycling, swimming, dancing, or strength training all count. Adults generally benefit from at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, plus muscle-strengthening work on two or more days, if appropriate for their health.

Rapid, restrictive plans often backfire. A safer approach is gradual change, adequate sleep, and support from a registered dietitian or clinician when needed. Do not use a BMI result to skip meals, overexercise, or start a supplement. If eating, weight, or body image feels distressing, compassionate professional support is available.

Nutrition, exercise, water, and sleep

There is no single meal plan for every body. A useful plate includes a source of protein, plants, and a satisfying carbohydrate. Strength exercise preserves muscle during weight loss and supports function during aging. Water needs vary with weather, food, activity, pregnancy, and health conditions; drink regularly and seek clinical advice if you have fluid restrictions. Sleep is often overlooked: a steady sleep schedule can support appetite regulation, energy, and recovery.

How to use this healthy weight calculator

Enter your age, sex, height, and weight. Choose metric or imperial units. The BMI calculator immediately displays your BMI value, category, and an estimated healthy-weight range for your height. Use the result as a point of orientation. If you have a chronic condition, are pregnant, are under 18, have had recent unexplained weight change, or are considering major changes to food or exercise, discuss the result with a qualified professional.
